records.remarks:
Fledgling (begging and flight call) following adult 'babysitter' male (song).

The recording was taken near the marshy pond at the East edge of Colony Farm Regional Park.   The weather was sunny, warm (20 C) with little or no wind.  I was standing about 5 meters away from the two birds.

The adult male and a juvenile (fledgling) Red-winged Blackbird were perched on top of a 3m high bush.  The adult male sang occasionally (heard at 0:00, 0:13, 0:31 and 0:43) while the juvenile was continuously begging (with wing fluttering).  The juvenile calls were directed away from the adult suggesting that the adult male was not actively involved in feeding the young bird.   Towards the end of the recording the adult flew down into the bulrushes (the original nest site perhaps) at which point the juvenile immediately followed switching to a different 3-syllable 'wait for me' flight call which can be heard at 0:52, 0:54 and 0:56, getting fainter as the birds distanced themselves from their bush-top perch and the microphone.

I watched the male adult and juvenile move back and forth between the bulrushes and the bush-top at least twice during the time that I was there.

A picture of the fledgling is available here: <http://www.flickr.com/photos/94309556@N05/8965154915/>

This is an interesting recording of an American Robin calling while aggressively chasing an adult Grey Jay (Perisoreus canadensis), recorded near the staff residences at Terra Nova National Park.

records.location: Happy Valley-Goose Bay, Division No. 10, Newfoundland and Labrador
records.remarks:
This is a very strange recording of a White-crowned Sparrow.  Rinchen Boardman and I came across this bird and puzzled over its identity for several minutes, before finally getting visual confirmation of it, and watching it sing its strange song through our binoculars.

Remarkably, this appears to be the first recording of White-crowned Sparrow from Labrador in the xeno-canto archive. However, it by no means is a typical song from this region. We heard many other White-crowned Sparrows in Goose Bay and on the eastern shore near Mary's Harbour, etc., that hardly resemble the bizarre monotonous song preserved in this recording.

records.remarks: Begging calls from single juvenile.  I have been watching the nest: this juvenile left the nest about 8 days ago.  It lacks flight feathers and spends most of the time hiding under dense shrubs.  At the beginning of the recording, the juvenile calls occasionally while the adult feeds on the open grass 5 to 10 meters away.  Toward the last portion of the recording, the adult returns to the juvenile, at which point the juvenile calls continuously, the adult opens its mouth, and juvenile feeds.  Afterwards, the adult departs and the begging calls cease.  I used a moderate high pass filter at  4000 Hz to reduce noise from three floatplanes.

records.location: Whistler, Squamish-Lillooet, British Columbia
records.remarks: This recording was not significantly modified. The White-crowned Sparrow in question here was observed in a fairly urban environment, particularly close to the Whistler Public Library and a road (you can hear a car starting in the recording). There is a small park nearby, with spruce and birch trees, as well as various shrubbery that I am not horticulturally skilled enough to name. I did not see the bird, I only heard it singing. I am fairly certain this was a male bird, but since female song is known from this species, and since I am unfamiliar with it, I'd prefer to leave this at "sex uncertain." The weather was clear, approaching sunset as I recall.
